verses.text: When David was a little past the top, behold, Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth met him with a couple of donkeys saddled, and on them two hundred loaves of bread, and one hundred clusters of raisins, and one hundred summer fruits, and a bottle of wine.

The king said to Ziba, “What do you mean by these?” Ziba said, “The donkeys are for the king’s household to ride on; and the bread and summer fruit for the young men to eat; and the wine, that those who are faint in the wilderness may drink.”
The king said, “Where is your master’s son?” Ziba said to the king, “Behold, he is staying in Jerusalem; for he said, ‘Today the house of Israel will restore me the kingdom of my father.’”
Then the king said to Ziba, “Behold, all that belongs to Mephibosheth is yours.” Ziba said, “I bow down. Let me find favor in your sight, my lord, O king.”
When king David came to Bahurim, behold, a man of the family of Saul’s house came out, whose name was Shimei, the son of Gera. He came out and cursed as he came.
He cast stones at David, and at all the servants of king David, and all the people and all the mighty men were on his right hand and on his left.
Shimei said when he cursed, “Be gone, be gone, you man of blood, and base fellow!

Yahweh has returned on you all the blood of Saul’s house, in whose place you have reigned! Yahweh has delivered the kingdom into the hand of Absalom your son! Behold, you are caught by your own mischief, because you are a man of blood!”
Then Abishai the son of Zeruiah said to the king, “Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Please let me go over and take off his head.”
The king said, “What have I to do with you, you sons of Zeruiah? Because he curses, and because Yahweh has said to him, ‘Curse David;’ who then shall say, ‘Why have you done so?’”

David said to Abishai, and to all his servants, “Behold, my son, who came out of my bowels, seeks my life. How much more this Benjamite, now? Leave him alone, and let him curse; for Yahweh has invited him.
It may be that Yahweh will look on the wrong done to me, and that Yahweh will repay me good for the cursing of me today.”
So David and his men went by the way; and Shimei went along on the hillside opposite him, and cursed as he went, threw stones at him, and threw dust.
The king, and all the people who were with him, came weary; and he refreshed himself there.
Absalom and all the people, the men of Israel, came to Jerusalem, and Ahithophel with him.
When Hushai the Archite, David’s friend, had come to Absalom, Hushai said to Absalom, “Long live the king! Long live the king!”
Absalom said to Hushai, “Is this your kindness to your friend? Why didn’t you go with your friend?”
Hushai said to Absalom, “No; but whomever Yahweh, and this people, and all the men of Israel have chosen, his will I be, and with him I will stay.
Again, whom should I serve? Shouldn’t I serve in the presence of his son? As I have served in your father’s presence, so will I be in your presence.”
Then Absalom said to Ahithophel, “Give your counsel what we shall do.”

Ahithophel said to Absalom, “Go in to your father’s concubines that he has left to keep the house. Then all Israel will hear that you are abhorred by your father. Then the hands of all who are with you will be strong.”
So they spread a tent for Absalom on the top of the house, and Absalom went in to his father’s concubines in the sight of all Israel.
The counsel of Ahithophel, which he gave in those days, was as if a man inquired at the inner sanctuary of God. So was all the counsel of Ahithophel both with David and with Absalom.

footnotes.content: Ziba meets the fleeing king with practical mercy—donkeys, bread, raisins, wine. The Lord often meets us not with grand comfort but with the exact gift we need at the moment we need it most. David is broken, and Ziba brings sustenance for a weary king.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "For the young men to eat; for those who are faint in the wilderness to drink." Even in exile, David's household must be tended. Every detail—who eats, who drinks—reminds us that God notices what we overlook when we're in crisis.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ziba accuses Mephibosheth of treason, claiming the old king's house seeks the throne for itself. We learn too late that words spoken in haste can destroy trust. This is a bitter lesson—words scatter like wind, and truth takes time to gather back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David rewards Ziba immediately without hearing Mephibosheth's side. Even good men make poor judgments when their hearts are full of pain. The Lord teaches us to wait before we speak, yet how often do we act first?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Bahurim, Shimei of Saul's house meets David with open hatred. Here is the voice of the past—old wounds that never healed, old grievances waiting in the shadows for their moment. They come when we are weakest.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Stones fly at David while his mighty men surround him. He is protected yet undefended against words. The fiercest weapons sometimes leave no blood, but they wound the spirit more deeply than any blade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be gone, you man of blood, and base fellow!" Shimei's curses are a mirror David fears—am I truly such a man? Self-doubt can be the enemy's sharpest stone when we are already fleeing our own failures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei declares the Lord has turned Saul's blood upon David and given the kingdom to Absalom. Here is a bitter truth wrapped in a curse—yes, David did what was necessary, yet the weight of it pursues him. Justice and mercy are never simple.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abishai burns for vengeance, wanting to silence the cursing mouth. We love the people we follow; when they are attacked, we want to strike back. But some battles are not ours to fight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: David asks, "Who can say 'Why have you done so?'" when God Himself has said 'Curse David'? This is a hard word—acceptance that even our sufferings may serve a purpose we cannot yet name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "My own son seeks my life. How much more this Benjamite?" David's wounds are nested—betrayal from his own blood makes every other wound bearable by comparison. Some griefs teach us mercy toward lesser hurts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Perhaps the Lord will look on my wrong and repay me good." Even as stones fly, David holds to hope that God sees. The Lord's eyes are always open, even when our enemies rage and we stumble in the dust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Shimei shadows them all the way, cursing, throwing stones and dust. Some afflictions walk beside us for a season. We cannot escape them, only endure them with our eyes fixed elsewhere.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The king and all his people came weary and refreshed themselves there. Even in flight, we must rest. The Lord does not ask us to run forever—He builds in the stopping places that sustain us for the road ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom enters Jerusalem. The rebellion moves from hiding to open throne. This is the moment the careful plots become a kingdom divided against itself—a house that cannot stand for long.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushai, David's friend, greets Absalom: "Long live the king!" Here begins the hidden work—a word spoken true enough on its surface yet sheltering a loyal heart underneath. God works through faithful men who know when to speak and when to hold their peace.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom questions Hushai's loyalty, wondering why he did not follow David. Trust between friends is tested in the fire—the one who serves well in hiding serves best.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hushai declares he will serve whomever the Lord and the people choose. A diplomat's answer—true, yet it conceals the deeper truth. Some servants of God must learn to speak in riddles to preserve what cannot be lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "As I served your father, so shall I serve you." Hushai turns his faithful history into a bridge toward Absalom. The past becomes a passport, and old loyalty becomes new cover. God's work in us often wears the clothes of yesterday.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Absalom turns to Ahithophel for counsel. Pride seeks out wisdom that will affirm its own desires. We are most dangerous when we gather around us only those who will say amen to our plans.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahithophel counsels Absalom to lie with David's concubines openly, burning every bridge and silencing any turning back. Wisdom without conscience becomes cruelty dressed in advice. The Lord grieves when knowledge serves only pride.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The deed is done in sight of all Israel. When wrong is done openly, everyone becomes a witness, and mercy becomes harder to find. Yet even this betrayal is known to God, and He does not forget His servant's broken heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo in this verse: we still turn to the counsel that sounds like divine wisdom when it is only ambition wearing a wise man's voice. The Lord teaches us to test all advice by the spirit of the Giver, not by the cleverness of the speaker.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
